traditions.title: Traditional Thai food and regional food culture
traditions.description: How do the staples and seasonings of central, northern, Isan and southern Thailand differ? A guide to Thailand's best-known dishes, regional flavours and what to know when you order for the first time.
traditions.eyebrow: Thai traditional food and food culture
traditions.h1: Even within one country,|the way people eat and the flavours differ
traditions.intro: If you have already tried Pad Thai and Tom Yum Kung, meet some other Thai dishes. In Chiang Mai, sticky rice comes with sausage, vegetables and a dipping sauce, while in Isan people enjoy a crunchy papaya salad and tangy fermented foods. Some dishes change from city to city, like the noodles and snacks of Phuket. Just as regional cooking differs across India, pick a new flavour in the city you travel to.
traditions.note: If Thai food is new to you, start with **a bowl of curry or noodles to eat with rice**. If you are with friends or family, share several dishes and enjoy the different flavours together.
basics: In the central region, rice is served with several dishes, while in the north and Isan people often eat sticky rice. Noodle dishes also differ by region.
Chilli, herbs, sour ingredients, fish seasoning and fermented ingredients are combined depending on the dish. The flavouring ingredients differ from dish to dish.
We introduce the main features of the central, northern, north-eastern Isan and southern regions. Within one region too, the food of each city and community differs.
Check **the ingredients of the seasonings and sauces** too. A dish called a vegetable dish or a chicken dish cannot tell you on its name alone whether it is vegetarian or halal.
traditions.regionsH2: Looking region by region makes the flavours clearer
traditions.orderH2: How to choose when you order for the first time
order: First decide whether you will share rice with side dishes or have a single bowl of noodles.
Choose the ingredients you want, such as meat, fish or prawns, and if there is any ingredient you avoid, tell the staff including the seasonings.
**Ask for the spice level before you order.** Soup or sauce that is already made can be hard to adjust.
When the food arrives, taste it first and then add extra seasoning and accompaniments a little at a time.
faq: Is all Thai food spicy?
Desserts and some dishes are not meant to be spicy. For curries and dipping sauces, colour or name alone does not tell you how spicy they are, so it helps to ask before you order.
Are regional specialities eaten only in that region?
Many dishes have spread to other regions and are eaten across the country. This guide explains the link with regional food culture and does not claim a place of origin or an exclusive area of sale.
Is a dish vegetarian if it has vegetables in it?
Animal-based seasonings such as fish sauce and shrimp paste are sometimes used. If you have a vegetarian requirement, ask the staff to tell you the actual ingredients, including the seasonings.

streetFood.intro: Enjoy a piece of warm roti and a cup of cold watermelon shake. In Thailand, the snacks and fruit drinks you have between meals are part of the fun of travel. From sweet snacks to sausage and fried chicken, find out how each dish tastes and how to eat it.

For drinks, look at the cup size and added ingredients, and if you want less sweetness, say so before it is made.
Look at the stall's menu and posted prices and order only the amount you need. You should not expect the same price or ingredients from a dish name alone.

fruitPrices.citiesH2: What to know when buying fruit in each city
fruitPrices.citiesText: Below are notes on choosing fruit on a trip to each city. **The prices shown as numbers are Bangkok retail survey values**, and we do not use them as ordinary street prices in other cities.
fruitPrices.compareH2: To compare on the same price list
compare: Look at variety, size and grade under the same conditions. For fruit with a thick rind, such as durian, ask whether the kg price includes the rind or is for the flesh only.
The size of one piece or the number in a bunch can differ. Do not convert to a per-kg price on your own; look at the amount you actually buy.
Look at the amount of flesh in one bag or pack. It differs from the weight of whole fruit with the rind.
Cup size, ingredients, and how much ice and syrup are used all differ. Do not compare the kg price of watermelon with a cup of watermelon shake as if they were the same product.

central.name: Central
central.subtitle: The central table, with curry served over rice
central.text: In the central region, curries and other dishes are served with rice. The richness of coconut milk, sourness, sweetness and heat blend differently in each dish. If you eat Tom Yum Kung and green curry in Bangkok, you can notice this mix of flavours.

north.name: North
north.subtitle: The north, with sticky rice and vegetables served with a dip
north.text: In the north, sticky rice and vegetables come with nam prik, and people also eat the herb-scented sai ua sausage. Chiang Mai's khao soi puts noodles and curry broth in one bowl. Not all northern food is mild, so ask about the spice level when you order.

isan.name: North-east · Isan
isan.subtitle: Isan, with crunchy papaya and tangy fermented food
isan.text: In Isan, try som tam and larb with sticky rice. Some dishes use pla ra, a fermented fish seasoning. Even within Isan, the chilli and seasoning used in som tam differ, so you can enjoy different flavours by area.

south.name: South
south.subtitle: The south, with seafood, noodles and many cultures on one table
south.text: In the south you can enjoy spicy food as well as noodles and snacks that differ from city to city. Phuket has dishes shaped by Chinese and Malay food culture, and in the Songkhla area the food of Chinese-descent and Muslim communities sits side by side. Pick the city you are visiting and look at its signature dishes.

bangkok.name: Bangkok
bangkok.tag: A city that gathers the flavours of the whole country
bangkok.intro: If you are choosing your first meal in Bangkok, start with Pad Thai. For the next meal, have curry with rice or share a Tom Yum Kung, and finish with sweet mango sticky rice. In Bangkok you can find food from many parts of Thailand, not only central Thai dishes.
bangkok.culture: Bangkok is a city where the food of many Thai regions comes together. The choice runs from central rice and curry to dishes brought from other regions. Here we introduce signature dishes that are easy to try, even if Bangkok is where you first meet Thai food.
bangkok.note: The dishes below are not local specialities eaten only in Bangkok. You can find them in many Thai cities.
bangkok.pairing: If you are eating alone, try a plate of Pad Thai or rice with curry. With friends or family, share a Tom Yum Kung and have a plate of mango sticky rice for dessert.
bangkok.priceGuide: In Bangkok, keep the per-kg price of whole fruit separate from the price of a pack of cut fruit. Below are official retail prices by variety and grade, surveyed on the same day. They can differ from the prices at individual shops in tourist areas.

chiang-mai.name: Chiang Mai
chiang-mai.tag: Lanna aromas and a sticky rice culture
chiang-mai.intro: In Chiang Mai, start northern food with a bowl of khao soi. You get soft noodles, crispy noodles and a rich curry broth together. For the next meal, have herb-scented sai ua and nam prik ong, a tomato dip, with sticky rice. It is a northern table quite different from a noodle dish.
chiang-mai.culture: In the north, sticky rice is eaten with several side dishes, vegetables and nam prik. The khantoke meal, with food laid out on a small tray table, also shows this food culture. Khantoke is not the name of one dish but of the table and style of dining in which several dishes are served.
chiang-mai.note: Khao soi, sai ua and nam prik ong are eaten not only in Chiang Mai but in other parts of the north too.
chiang-mai.pairing: If you want a light lunch, choose khao soi. On a day of sharing several dishes, order sai ua, nam prik ong, sticky rice and vegetables together for a northern Thai meal.
chiang-mai.priceGuide: In Chiang Mai, look at longan and lychee, which are linked to the north. For fruit sold by the bunch, it helps to ask whether the weight includes the stalks. Keep dried longan and fresh fruit separate, by product and pack weight.

phuket.name: Phuket
phuket.tag: Noodles and snacks shaped by Chinese and Malay culture
phuket.intro: In Phuket you need not stop at grilled seafood. Try mi hokkien, thick noodles stir-fried, and mi hun, thin rice noodles. After the meal, take a break with o-aew, a bowl of ice and jelly. Add local food to the day you spend walking the old town.
phuket.culture: Phuket's food carries the influence of Chinese-descent and Malay food culture. Thick noodles are sometimes stir-fried with seafood, and thin noodles may come with a pork rib broth. When you also look at the snack eaten with ice and jelly, Phuket's table looks more varied than the seafood you may have expected.
phuket.note: Mi hokkien and mi hun are different noodle dishes. If you order them by name, you can enjoy the difference in texture and in what comes with each.
phuket.pairing: Have mi hokkien or mi hun as your meal, and on a hot day choose o-aew for dessert. If you are in a group, share the two noodle dishes and compare thick noodles with thin ones.
phuket.priceGuide: In Phuket, keep cut fruit or a drink that you eat right on the beach separate from whole fruit. If you convert the price of a bag or a cup into a per-kg price of whole fruit to compare, the amount you actually eat can differ.

ayutthaya.name: Ayutthaya
ayutthaya.tag: River food and roti sai mai
ayutthaya.intro: In Ayutthaya, have boat noodles for lunch between the ruins. If you want to share a meal with your group, you could pick grilled river prawns. Roti sai mai, thin roti wrapped around sugar threads, is a snack to try in Ayutthaya. Wrap each piece yourself and enjoy a sweet moment on your trip.
ayutthaya.culture: Ayutthaya, close to the river, is well known for a food trip of noodles and river prawns. You can also try roti sai mai, which Muslim communities have kept alive. Eat a meal of noodles and wrap roti around sugar threads, and enjoy two quite different dishes of the same city.
ayutthaya.note: Boat noodles are eaten in other cities too. River prawns cost different amounts depending on size and selling unit, so choose by looking at the prawns you will order.
ayutthaya.pairing: Have boat noodles at lunch, and for a group meal share grilled river prawns with rice. Roti sai mai is good to wrap one piece at a time, adjusting the amount of sugar threads.
ayutthaya.priceGuide: On a day of sightseeing the ruins in Ayutthaya, first decide how much fruit you will eat right away. Units differ by fruit, such as a bunch for bananas and kg for whole watermelon. For prepared fruit in a bag or pack, look at the amount and the price together.

khon-kaen.name: Khon Kaen
khon-kaen.tag: Isan's fermented flavours and freshwater fish dishes
khon-kaen.intro: In Khon Kaen, enjoy Isan food with som tam and larb along with sticky rice. In one meal you share crunchy papaya, rich meat and a tangy dressing. Also look at sai krok Isan, a fermented sausage, and au pla, a freshwater fish curry. They are dishes whose ingredients and way of eating differ even within one region.
khon-kaen.culture: In Isan, sticky rice and fermented seasonings are used widely in food. The ways of building flavour vary, from som tam, in which papaya is pounded, to larb with herbs and toasted rice powder and a sausage of fermented rice and pork. We also introduce au pla, a local dish of Khon Kaen that uses freshwater fish.
khon-kaen.note: Som tam, larb and sai krok Isan are eaten in many parts of Isan. Au pla is introduced as a local dish of Khon Kaen.
khon-kaen.pairing: When you eat som tam or larb, order sticky rice too. If the smell of fermentation is unfamiliar, it helps to ask first whether the som tam has pla ra in it. On a day when you want fish rather than meat, look at au pla.
khon-kaen.priceGuide: In Khon Kaen, tell apart ripe papaya, eaten as fruit, and green papaya, used in som tam. When you buy whole fruit, look at the per-kg price and the total weight, and for cut fruit look at the amount in one pack.

hat-yai.name: Hat Yai
hat-yai.tag: Fried chicken and soup dishes of the Songkhla area
hat-yai.intro: In Hat Yai, try fried chicken served with fried shallots. Eaten together, the chicken and shallots give crunch and a rich aroma. When you want a different meal, you could also choose bak kut teh, a herb-scented pork rib soup. Meet the varied food culture of the Songkhla area one dish at a time.
hat-yai.culture: The Songkhla area, where Hat Yai lies, has the food of Chinese-descent and Muslim communities side by side. There are meals of sticky rice with fried chicken, and meals of bak kut teh with its Chinese-style herb aroma. The meat and seasoning differ from dish to dish, so choose a menu together that everyone in your group can eat.
hat-yai.note: Bak kut teh is not introduced as a dish that began in Hat Yai. Even for a chicken dish, you cannot decide on the name alone whether it is halal.
hat-yai.pairing: Eat the fried chicken with sticky rice. Eat the fried shallots with the chicken, and add the sauce a little at a time. On a day when you want a warm soup meal, choose bak kut teh made with pork ribs.
hat-yai.priceGuide: In Hat Yai, also look at the growing-area seasons of southern fruit. Even the same rambutan or mangosteen comes into season differently by area. When you buy a single bag, ask for the weight in it and the total price together.

pad-thai.name: Pad Thai
pad-thai.intro: If you are wondering what to eat first in Thailand, try Pad Thai. Rice noodles are stir-fried with egg and tofu in a sweet and tangy tamarind sauce. Crunchy bean sprouts and rich peanuts give you several textures on one plate. Squeeze the lime served with it lightly over the noodles and the tang comes out more.
pad-thai.flavor: The sourness of tamarind blends with sweet and salty notes. Chew the bean sprouts and peanuts with the soft noodles and you get a crunchy, nutty taste. Where chilli flakes are served on the side, you can add as much as you like.
pad-thai.ingredients: Rice noodles with egg, tofu and bean sprouts, flavoured with tamarind. Prawns, dried shrimp and peanuts are sometimes used, so if there is an ingredient you avoid, tell the staff before you order.
pad-thai.story: Pad Thai is Thailand's best-known stir-fried noodle dish. It is easy to find in Bangkok, but it is not a local speciality eaten only there. If Thai food is new to you, start with Pad Thai, and for the next meal try a noodle dish with broth, such as khao soi.
pad-thai.tip: If you do not eat prawns, ask whether dried shrimp is also in the seasoning.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as prawns, and order. If you do not eat prawns, ask whether dried shrimp is added too.
When the dish arrives, try it as it is first. Add the lime and peanuts a little at a time to adjust the tang and richness to your taste.
If you like heat, add a little chilli flakes. If egg or peanuts must be left out, tell the staff before the dish is cooked.
faq: Does Pad Thai always have prawns?

No. The main ingredient depends on the menu item. But even when no prawns are visible, dried shrimp is sometimes used in the seasoning, so if you cannot eat prawns, ask about both the main ingredient and the seasoning.
Can I eat it only in Bangkok?
No. It is a signature dish eaten in many Thai cities. On a Bangkok trip, it is a good first meal for getting used to Thai food.

tom-yum-kung.name: Tom Yum Kung
tom-yum-kung.intro: Try Tom Yum Kung, a hot soup in which the aroma of lemongrass and kaffir lime leaf rises from the broth. It is Thailand's best-known soup, cooked sour and spicy with prawns. A spoonful brings sourness, heat and herbs together. If you are eating with friends or family, order rice and share a bowl of Tom Yum Kung.
tom-yum-kung.flavor: Sourness and heat are added to a broth that has taken on the flavour of prawns. Lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaf give Tom Yum Kung its distinctive aroma. There are clear and rich versions, so dishes with the same name can taste a little different.
tom-yum-kung.ingredients: Prawns, with aroma from lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaf and more. The seasoning and the broth differ with the recipe.
tom-yum-kung.story: Tom Yum Kung is a dish whose recipe has been passed on in homes and communities. The cooking knowledge and culture around it were added to the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024. This is not a certification of any one restaurant but a recognition of the culture that people have handed down by making and sharing the dish.
tom-yum-kung.tip: If you do not eat prawns, choose another dish instead of Tom Yum Kung.
steps: Look at whether the menu offers a clear or a rich broth, and choose. If you want less heat, say so when you order. Broth that is already cooked can be hard to adjust.
Take the broth in small spoonfuls with rice. If you are in a group, serve it into each bowl and share the prawns and broth.
The hard lemongrass stalks and aromatics in the broth are there for flavour. Pick out the pieces you will eat along with the prawns.
faq: Is it a restaurant that was listed by UNESCO?
No. What was listed is the knowledge of making Tom Yum Kung and the related food culture. It does not mean that any restaurant has been certified.
Is every tom yum a prawn soup?
No. Kung means prawn, and there are also tom yum soups made with other ingredients. The name that follows tom yum on the menu helps you choose the main ingredient.
emphasis: If you do not eat prawns

green-curry.name: Green Curry
green-curry.scope: Central food culture · eaten across the country
green-curry.intro: If you want a fragrant curry with rice, choose green curry. Green curry paste is stirred into coconut milk and simmered with meat and vegetables. Basil-like herbs add aroma to the richness of coconut. The pale green colour looks mild, but it does have heat, so if you do not handle spicy food well, say so when you order.
green-curry.flavor: Behind the rich, soft coconut milk you feel the heat of the curry paste. The herb aroma is also clear, so it tastes different from the curries you may know from home. Eat it by putting a little curry and its pieces on the rice at a time.
green-curry.ingredients: Made with green curry paste and coconut milk, simmered with meat and vegetables. Herbs such as basil are sometimes added for aroma.
green-curry.story: Green curry is one of the signature dishes of central Thailand. In Thailand it is eaten not only with steamed rice but also with noodles such as khanom chin, or with roti. On a Bangkok trip, have a meal of curry with the meat you like and rice on the side.
green-curry.tip: Even with coconut milk, it has heat. Ask about the spice level when you order.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as chicken, and order. If curry and rice are sold separately, order the rice too.
Ask before the dish is made whether the heat can be reduced. Even with coconut milk, it is not a dish without heat.
Put the curry broth and pieces on the rice a little at a time. If you are sharing several dishes, you do not need to pour all the curry over the rice at once.
faq: Is green curry not spicy?
It has heat. Even if the coconut milk makes it feel soft, the curry paste uses chilli. If you do not handle spicy food well, it helps to ask about the spice level before you order.
Is a curry with only vegetables a vegetarian dish?
Not necessarily. Animal-based ingredients can go into the curry paste or the seasonings. If you are vegetarian, ask whether the paste and the sauce can be eaten as well as the meat.
emphasis: Even with coconut milk, it has heat
green-curry.photoAlt: Green curry in a bowl served with roti
green-curry.photoCaption: Green curry with roti · example dish

massaman.name: Massaman Curry
massaman.intro: Try massaman curry, with the aroma of cinnamon and cardamom. It is a rich curry flavoured with several spices, good to eat slowly with rice. It also suits anyone who wants to notice a different aroma from green curry. It is known as a relatively mild curry, but the heat differs from shop to shop.
massaman.flavor: The aroma of spices such as cinnamon, cardamom and clove soaks into the curry. If you eat it next to green curry, where herbs stand out, you can easily feel the difference between the two. Eat the rich sauce with rice, a little at a time.
massaman.ingredients: Flavoured with several spices such as cinnamon, cardamom and clove. The actual ingredients, such as meat and nuts, depend on the menu item you order.
massaman.story: Massaman is one of Thailand's signature curries and is also introduced in guides to central food culture. It is not a dish eaten only in one city. If Thai curry is new to you, start with massaman, and when you become curious about the flavour of herbs and chilli, try green curry too.
massaman.tip: A relatively mild curry does not mean it has no heat.
steps: Choose a menu item with the meat you want. It also helps to see whether rice to eat with the curry is included.
Take a little curry first and then have it with rice. Put the rich sauce and the meat on the rice together.
If you cannot eat nuts or a particular spice, tell the staff before you order. Even a relatively mild curry can have heat.
faq: I am new to Thai curry. Is massaman a good one to try?
It is worth choosing if you want to begin with a relatively mild curry. But the heat and the spice flavour differ from shop to shop, so ask about the spice level when you order.
Is every massaman halal?
You cannot decide whether a dish is halal from its name alone. Please check the meat and seasonings used, along with the restaurant's certification.
emphasis: does not mean it has no heat

mango-sticky-rice.name: Mango Sticky Rice
mango-sticky-rice.intro: If you want something sweet after a meal, try mango sticky rice. It is a Thai dessert in which sticky rice flavoured with coconut milk is served next to ripe mango. Eat mango and sticky rice together in one bite and the fruit's sweetness blends with the chewy texture. If you have finished a full meal, share a plate with your companion.
mango-sticky-rice.flavor: The sweetness of mango is joined by the richness of coconut. The sticky rice is chewy, so the texture differs from eating the fruit alone. Taste the mango and the sticky rice separately, and next time take them together in one spoonful.
mango-sticky-rice.ingredients: Ripe mango served with sticky rice flavoured with coconut milk. The sauce and toppings differ from seller to seller.
mango-sticky-rice.story: In Thailand, sticky rice flavoured with coconut milk is eaten as a dessert with various toppings. Mango sticky rice is the version served with ripe mango. It contains rice, but think of it as a sweet dessert rather than a meal eaten with side dishes.
mango-sticky-rice.tip: It contains rice, but it is a dish enjoyed as a sweet dessert.
steps: If you have already finished a meal, look at the size of the plate and decide whether to share it.
Take a bite of the mango and of the sticky rice separately, then eat them together. You can feel how the taste and texture change when the two meet.
If the sauce is served separately, add it a little at a time. You do not need to pour it all on from the start.
faq: It has rice in it. Is it eaten as a meal?
It is usually enjoyed as a sweet dessert. Mango is eaten together with sticky rice flavoured with coconut milk. If you have it after a meal, you can share it with your companion.
Does the mango always taste the same?
No. It depends on the variety, how ripe it is and when it is sold. The dish is the mango's flavour with sticky rice and coconut sauce added, so try them together bite by bite.

khao-soi.name: Khao Soi
khao-soi.intro: If you are choosing a meal in Chiang Mai, try khao soi. It is a signature northern dish of egg noodles in a coconut curry broth, topped with crispy fried noodles. There is fun in alternating soft noodles and crunchy noodles. If lime comes on the side, taste the broth first and then squeeze in a little.
khao-soi.flavor: The rich curry broth and the texture of two kinds of noodles are its character. The noodles on top are crunchy at first and slowly soften as they touch the broth. Taste the broth before and after adding the accompaniments, and you can enjoy different flavours in one bowl.
khao-soi.ingredients: Egg noodles in a coconut curry broth, with fried noodles on top. Some menus let you choose the main ingredient, such as chicken or beef.
khao-soi.story: Khao soi is a well-known dish on a Chiang Mai trip, but it is eaten in other northern cities too. Unlike the northern meal laid out with sticky rice and side dishes, noodles and broth come in one bowl. It is a good choice when you are eating alone or want a light lunch.
khao-soi.tip: Try the crunchy noodles on top first, before they get wet in the broth.
steps: Choose the main ingredient you want, such as chicken or beef, and order.
Take a bite of the fried noodles first, before they get wet in the broth. Alternating with the soft noodles below lets you feel the difference in texture.
Taste the broth first, then add the lime and accompaniments a little at a time. You do not need to add everything from the start.
faq: Can I eat it only in Chiang Mai?
No. It is a signature dish eaten in many northern cities. If you are meeting northern food for the first time in Chiang Mai, you could start with a bowl of khao soi.
What meat goes into khao soi?
There are several menu items, such as chicken or beef. Look at the main ingredient written on the menu and choose what you want. Not every shop uses the same meat.
khao-soi.photoAlt: Khao soi topped with fried noodles with accompaniments served separately

sai-ua.name: Sai Ua
sai-ua.intro: If you want a fragrant meat dish in Chiang Mai, choose sai ua. It is a northern sausage of pork mixed with chilli and herbs and then grilled. One slice gives you the richness of grilled meat and the aroma of herbs together. With sticky rice and vegetables it makes a good northern Thai meal.
sai-ua.flavor: The richness of pork is joined by the aroma of herbs and chilli seasoning. Its character is an aroma different from the sausages you know. The heat varies with the recipe, so if it is your first time, you can start with a small piece.
sai-ua.ingredients: Pork mixed with chilli, garlic and several herbs, then grilled. The blend of herbs and seasoning differs from maker to maker.
sai-ua.story: Sai ua often appears on the table of Lanna in the north. It is sometimes eaten with sticky rice or with a dipping sauce such as nam prik. Ordered with nam prik ong, which is flavoured with tomato, and vegetables, you can alternate between the grilled meat and the sauce.
sai-ua.tip: It is a sausage of pork mixed with herbs and grilled.
steps: Choose the amount you will eat and order. If you are sharing several dishes, you can share a little with your companion.
Start with a small piece. Once you know the herb aroma and the heat, it is easier to decide how much sticky rice or vegetables to eat with it.
Eat it with sticky rice, nam prik and vegetables. You get a different meal from eating the sausage alone.
faq: Is it the same sausage as sai krok Isan?
No. Sai ua is a northern sausage grilled with herbs. Sai krok Isan is an Isan dish made by fermenting pork and rice, and its character is the tang that comes from fermentation.
Can I order it if I do not eat pork?
The standard sai ua is made with pork. If you do not eat pork, it is better to choose another dish for your meal.

nam-prik-ong.name: Nam Phrik Ong
nam-prik-ong.intro: Meet nam prik ong, eaten with vegetables at a northern meal. It is a red dipping sauce made from tomato, minced pork and chilli. Dab a little on vegetables or eat it with sticky rice and you get the savoury depth of pork and the tang of tomato together. Order it with sai ua and set a northern Thai table.
nam-prik-ong.flavor: The tang of tomato and the savoury depth of pork are joined by chilli seasoning. When the soft sauce goes with crunchy vegetables, different textures blend. The heat differs from maker to maker.
nam-prik-ong.ingredients: Made with tomato, minced pork and chilli. It is a sauce eaten a little at a time with sticky rice and vegetables.
nam-prik-ong.story: Nam prik is a dipping sauce eaten with vegetables or rice in Thailand. The north has several nam prik, and nam prik ong is the kind that uses tomato and pork. It can also be met together with sticky rice and vegetables at a khantoke meal, with food laid out on a small tray table.
nam-prik-ong.tip: Even a tomato sauce has minced pork in it.
steps: See whether sticky rice and vegetables come with it, and order it together with other northern dishes.
Dab a little sauce on vegetables and try it first. With sticky rice you can enjoy it in another texture.
Even though it is a tomato sauce, it is a dish that uses pork. If you avoid meat or animal-based seasonings, tell the staff before you order.
faq: Is it a vegetarian dish if it is made with tomato?
No. The standard nam prik ong contains minced pork. If you are vegetarian, do not choose it by the tomato colour alone, but ask about the meat and the seasonings.
Do you eat the sauce on its own?
It is eaten a little at a time with vegetables, sticky rice and so on. Ordered with a grilled dish such as sai ua, it is easy to share several flavours.
nam-prik-ong.photoAlt: Nam prik ong, a tomato and pork sauce, with vegetables

mi-hokkien.name: Mi Hokkien
mi-hokkien.scope: A local noodle dish of Phuket
mi-hokkien.intro: If you want a noodle dish in Phuket, try mi hokkien. Thick yellow noodles are stir-fried over high heat with seafood and sauce. You taste the sauce soaked into the noodles and the seafood together. It is a good lunch to choose on a day you walk around Phuket Old Town.
mi-hokkien.flavor: The flavour of sauce and seafood soaks into the thick noodles. Compared with mi hun, which uses thin rice noodles, the texture of the noodles feels different. The taste of a bowl can also change with the amount of broth and accompaniments such as egg.
mi-hokkien.ingredients: Thick yellow noodles stir-fried with seafood and sauce. Meat or egg is sometimes used too, so look at the other ingredients listed on the menu.
mi-hokkien.story: Phuket's food carries the food culture handed down by Chinese-descent residents. Mi hokkien is a signature noodle dish shaped by that influence. If you had thought of Phuket only as grilled seafood, enjoy a different meal with this dish, in which seafood and noodles are stir-fried together.
mi-hokkien.tip: It is a different noodle dish from mi hun, which uses thin rice noodles.
steps: Look at which ingredients go in, such as seafood, meat or egg, and choose the menu item you want.
When it arrives, eat the noodles and seafood together. You can taste the sauce soaked into the thick noodles.
If extra seasoning is served, taste first and then add a little at a time. If you cannot eat seafood, ask whether it is also in the stock and the sauce.
faq: Is it the same noodle dish as mi hun?

No. Mi hokkien is a signature Phuket noodle dish that uses thick yellow noodles, while mi hun uses thin rice noodles. Try both and you can feel that the texture of the noodles and what is served with them differ.
Can I order it if I cannot eat seafood?
The standard mi hokkien contains seafood. Whether the ingredients can be changed differs from shop to shop, so you need to ask about the stock and the sauce, not only the main ingredient.
emphasis: different noodle dish from mi hun

mi-hun.name: Mi Hun
mi-hun.scope: A local noodle dish of Phuket
mi-hun.intro: In Phuket, also try mi hun, thin rice noodles. It is known as a dish served with a pork rib broth. Take a bite of noodles and then a spoonful of warm broth, and you get a different taste from eating the noodles alone. Choose it when you are curious about another noodle dish after the thick-noodle mi hokkien.
mi-hun.flavor: It is a dish in which you enjoy the texture of thin rice noodles with the flavour of the broth served alongside. If the noodles and broth come separately, alternate between them. It gives you a different meal from thick stir-fried noodles.
mi-hun.ingredients: Made with thin rice noodles. The form served together with a pork rib broth is well known.
mi-hun.story: In Phuket you can find thin rice noodle dishes under names such as mi hun and mi hun ba chang. Serving them with a pork rib broth is the well-known form. The way it is served can differ from shop to shop, so look at the menu to see whether noodles and broth come together.
mi-hun.tip: Look at whether the pork rib broth comes with it before you order.
steps: Look at the menu to see whether the pork rib broth comes with it, and order.
Take a bite of the noodles first, then a spoonful of the warm broth. Enjoy the noodles and broth by turns.
If you do not eat pork, ask about the ingredients in the noodle seasoning and the broth together. Do not assume you can avoid pork just by leaving out the broth.
faq: Do the noodles and broth always come together?
It differs by shop and menu item. Serving with a pork rib broth is the well-known form, but it helps to look at what is included in the menu item you order.
If I do not eat pork, can I just leave out the broth?
Pork can also be used in the seasoning or cooking of the noodles. If you avoid pork, you need to ask about the ingredients of both the noodles and the broth.

o-aew.name: O-Aew
o-aew.intro: If you are walking the old town on a hot day in Phuket and want a short break, try o-aew. It is a cold snack in which jelly, sweet syrup and toppings are put on ice. Scoop the ice and jelly together and you get coolness and a soft texture. It also works as dessert after a noodle meal.
o-aew.flavor: The sweetness of soft jelly and syrup is added to cold ice. The taste and texture of each spoonful change with which toppings go on. Scoop the ice and jelly together and try it.
o-aew.ingredients: Ice and jelly with sweet syrup and toppings added. What the jelly and toppings are made from differs from shop to shop.
o-aew.story: O-aew is a local dessert of Phuket. Phuket's table has not only seafood and noodle dishes but also cold snacks like this. It is worth choosing when you look for something sweet between meals on your trip.
o-aew.tip: Scoop the ice and jelly together and you can enjoy both textures.
steps: Look at which jelly and toppings go on, and choose. You can also ask whether the syrup can be adjusted.
Take a spoonful of ice and jelly together. You can enjoy a different texture from eating the jelly alone.
If there is an ingredient you avoid, ask what the jelly and toppings are made from. Even when sold under the same name, the makeup is not the same everywhere.
faq: Is o-aew eaten as a meal?
It is a snack made with ice and jelly. Have it as a short break on a hot day, or as dessert after a meal.
Are the jelly and toppings the same everywhere?
No. The toppings and syrup can differ from shop to shop. If there is an ingredient you cannot eat, ask about the jelly and the toppings together.

boat-noodles.name: Boat Noodles
boat-noodles.intro: If a bowl of noodles sounds good while you tour the ruins in Ayutthaya, try boat noodles. Noodles and meat are served in broth, and together with grilled river prawns it is famous in Ayutthaya. Choose the noodles and meat from the menu and enjoy it with the broth while it is warm. It is eaten in other cities too, but it is a good meal to choose on an Ayutthaya trip.
boat-noodles.flavor: It is a dish in which you enjoy broth, noodles and meat together. The taste of the broth can change with the meat and seasoning. Try it first without adding seasoning, then add chilli or other seasoning a little at a time.
boat-noodles.ingredients: Noodles and meat served in broth. How meat, offal and seasonings are used differs from menu item to menu item.
boat-noodles.story: On a food trip in Ayutthaya you can meet boat noodles, grilled river prawns and roti sai mai together. A plan of a noodle meal at lunch and roti sai mai as a snack also works well. But boat noodles can be eaten in places other than Ayutthaya too.
boat-noodles.tip: Order by looking at the noodle type, the meat and the bowl size.
steps: Choose the noodles and meat you want, and order. If you avoid meat, offal or a particular seasoning, ask about the ingredients in the broth too.
Look at the bowl size and decide how many bowls to eat. Not every shop serves the same size.
Taste the broth first, then add extra seasoning a little at a time. You do not need to add a lot of chilli from the start.
faq: Can I eat it only in Ayutthaya?
No. It is a dish eaten in other cities too. In Ayutthaya you could choose it as a meal between visits to the ruins.
Are the ingredients in the broth all the same?
No. The meat, offal, seasonings and broth differ by menu item. If there is an ingredient you avoid, ask whether it is also used in the broth rather than only asking to leave out the meat.

river-prawns.name: Grilled River Prawns
river-prawns.intro: If you are looking for a meal to share in Ayutthaya, choose grilled river prawns. Prawns are grilled and the meat is picked out to eat, and it suits a group eating with rice and other dishes. The price differs with prawn size and selling unit, so look at the prawns you will order first and then choose.
river-prawns.flavor: It is a dish in which you enjoy the aroma of grilled prawns and the texture of the meat. Try the meat alone first, then add a little of the sauce served with it. Eaten with rice, you enjoy the flavour of the sauce too.
river-prawns.ingredients: River prawns are grilled. Prawn size, the sauce served and the selling unit differ from restaurant to restaurant.
river-prawns.story: River prawns are a well-known food ingredient on an Ayutthaya trip. If boat noodles are a one-bowl meal, grilled river prawns can be chosen as a dish to share with your companions. You need not assume from the name river prawns alone that they are wild or caught in the rivers of Ayutthaya.
river-prawns.tip: Ask whether the selling unit is per prawn or by weight.
steps: First ask whether the price is per prawn or by weight. Even for the same grilled prawns, the amount differs by size and selling method.
Decide the size and number of prawns and get the price for your order. It also helps to see whether rice and other dishes are included.
Pick out the prawn meat and try it as it is first. Add a little sauce and share with your companions.
faq: Are they all prawns caught in the rivers of Ayutthaya?
You cannot tell from the dish name alone. If you want to know the actual origin and whether they are farmed, ask about the prawns you are going to order.
How much will it cost?
It depends on the selling method, such as prawn size and per prawn or by weight. If you get the price for the size and number you chose before you order, it is easy to settle the cost of the meal.
river-prawns.photoAlt: Split and grilled river prawns with sauce

roti-sai-mai.name: Roti Sai Mai
roti-sai-mai.intro: In Ayutthaya, try roti sai mai, thin roti wrapped around sugar threads. It is a snack in which fine sugar threads are put on roti and rolled up to eat. When you wrap it yourself, you can add the sugar threads a little at a time and enjoy the sweetness you like. You could also open the roti one sheet at a time and share with your companion.
roti-sai-mai.flavor: The texture of thin, soft roti and fine sugar threads blend. The sweetness depends on how many sugar threads you add. Add only a little at first, and on the next roti add more to your taste.
roti-sai-mai.ingredients: Thin roti wrapped around fine sugar threads. There are also versions in which pandan aroma or sesame seeds are added to the roti.
roti-sai-mai.story: Roti sai mai is linked to the snack culture that Ayutthaya's Muslim community has kept alive. Some roti gets a green colour from pandan aroma, and some uses sesame seeds. Unlike an ordinary roti menu, wrapping the sugar threads is the character of this snack.
roti-sai-mai.tip: Add the sugar threads a little at a time and you can eat it at the sweetness you like.
steps: Get the roti and sugar threads together. If they are served separately, open out one sheet of roti.
Put on a little sugar thread, then roll or fold the roti and try it.
If you need more sweetness, add a little more sugar threads to the next roti. You do not need to add a lot at once.
faq: How is it different from ordinary roti?
It is a dish in which thin roti is wrapped around fine sugar threads. The way of eating and the texture differ from roti with banana or other toppings.
Is green roti the same snack?
There is also a form in which roti with pandan aroma is wrapped around sugar threads. The actual aroma and ingredients can differ from seller to seller.
roti-sai-mai.photoAlt: Fine sugar threads on thin roti

som-tam.name: Som Tam
som-tam.scope: A signature Isan dish · eaten across the country
som-tam.intro: If you want something crunchy and tangy, try som tam. It is a salad made by cutting unripe papaya into thin strips and pounding it with seasoning in a mortar. The papaya soaks up sourness and heat, and it goes well with sticky rice or grilled food. In Isan some versions use a fermented fish seasoning, so if the smell of fermentation is unfamiliar, ask which kind of som tam it is when you order.
som-tam.flavor: Sour and spicy seasoning blends with the crunch of papaya. In the versions that use pla ra, a fermented fish seasoning, you can also notice the smell of fermentation. Even with the same som tam, the taste differs with how the seasoning and chilli are used.
som-tam.ingredients: Unripe papaya seasoned with chilli and souring ingredients. Peanuts, dried shrimp and fermented fish seasoning depend on the kind of som tam.
som-tam.story: Som tam is a signature dish of Isan and is eaten in many Thai cities. Even within Isan, each area has different kinds, so you can compare the taste of som tam just as regional cooking differs across India. On a Khon Kaen trip, have it with sticky rice and other Isan dishes.
som-tam.tip: If you want less heat, say so before it is made.
steps: Choose the kind of som tam and ask whether a fermented fish seasoning such as pla ra goes in.
If you want less heat, say so before it is made. Once the papaya has been pounded with the seasoning, it is hard to take out only the chilli.
Order sticky rice and other dishes together and eat a little of each at a time. You get a different meal from eating papaya alone.
faq: Does som tam taste the same wherever you eat it?
No. The chilli and seasoning used and the way of adding sweetness differ. If the smell of fermentation is unfamiliar, it helps to ask first whether pla ra goes in.
It is a papaya salad, so is it vegetarian?
Not necessarily. Some kinds use fish seasoning or dried shrimp. If you are vegetarian, ask whether the seasoning and toppings other than papaya can be eaten.

larb.name: Larb
larb.intro: If you are looking for a meat dish to eat with sticky rice, try Isan-style larb. Minced meat is seasoned with herbs, lime and toasted rice powder. Sourness and a nutty aroma are added to the taste of the meat, and it goes well with vegetables. Some versions use raw meat, so when you order, ask whether the larb is made with cooked meat.
larb.flavor: The sourness of lime and the aroma of herbs are joined by the nutty taste of toasted rice powder. The seasoning is mixed evenly through the minced meat, so it is easy to eat a little at a time with sticky rice. The taste also differs with the meat used, such as pork, beef or duck.
larb.ingredients: Minced meat seasoned with toasted rice powder, herbs, lime and more. The kind of meat differs, such as pork, beef or duck.
larb.story: Larb is a meat salad met at the Isan table. There is larb in the north too, but the seasoning and cooking method are not the same. The dish introduced here is Isan-style larb, with toasted rice powder, lime and herbs added.
larb.tip: Some kinds use raw meat. Order larb that is made with cooked meat.
steps: Choose the meat you want and order it as a cooked dish. There is also larb that uses raw meat.
If you want less heat, say so before the dish is made.
Have it with sticky rice and vegetables. Share the larb a little at a time and enjoy the flavour of the meat and herbs.
faq: Is larb always made with cooked meat?
No. Some kinds use raw meat. The Tourism Authority of Thailand advises ordering larb made with cooked meat, so say so when you order.
Does northern larb taste the same?

The seasoning and cooking method differ. Here we introduce Isan-style larb, which uses toasted rice powder, lime and herbs. Even when you see the same name in the north, it can feel like a different dish.
larb.photoCaption: Isan-style larb made with duck · example dish

sai-krok-isan.name: Sai Krok Isan
sai-krok-isan.intro: If you want to taste the tangy fermented food of Isan, try sai krok Isan. It is a sausage made by mixing pork, rice, garlic and more and letting it ferment. The sourness that comes from fermentation is added to the rich taste of the meat. If you have tried sai ua, the northern sausage, you could compare the taste of the two.
sai-krok-isan.flavor: Its character is the richness of pork and the tang that comes from fermentation. The strength of the sourness differs with the degree of fermentation and the cooking method. The raw chillies served with it can be hot, so try them on the side a little at a time.
sai-krok-isan.ingredients: Pork, rice, garlic and more are mixed and fermented. The sourness can change with the fermentation and cooking method.
sai-krok-isan.story: Sai krok Isan is an Isan dish made by fermenting pork and rice. It is not a dish eaten only in Khon Kaen. Compared with the northern sai ua, which enjoys herb aroma, you can feel how the ingredients and taste of sausage differ by region.
sai-krok-isan.tip: Try the raw chillies served with it on the side, a little at a time.
steps: Order sai ua, which uses herbs, and sai krok Isan, the fermented sausage, as separate dishes.
Try the cooked sausage a little at a time. Tasting first tells you how strong the fermented tang is.
If raw chillies come with it, rather than eating them all at once, try them on the side a little at a time.
faq: Why does a sausage taste sour?
Because it is made by fermenting pork and rice. It is a sausage that enjoys the tang from fermentation, and the actual strength of the sourness depends on the product and the cooking method.
How is it different from sai ua?

Sai ua is a northern sausage grilled with herbs, while sai krok Isan is an Isan sausage in which pork and rice are fermented. Try both and you can compare the herb aroma with the sour taste of fermentation.

au-pla.name: Au Pla
au-pla.scope: A local dish of Khon Kaen
au-pla.intro: If you want to try a regional dish other than som tam in Khon Kaen, look for au pla. It is a spicy, salty curry made with freshwater fish. If you like fish dishes, it is worth choosing as a meal to eat with rice. The fish and seasoning used can differ from shop to shop.
au-pla.flavor: It is a curry in which heat and saltiness are added to freshwater fish. It gives you a different meal from a dish of crunchy vegetables such as som tam, or a meat dish such as larb. Eat it with rice, adding a little at a time.
au-pla.ingredients: A curry made with freshwater fish. The fish and the seasoning used depend on the menu item you order.
au-pla.story: Isan has a culture of using freshwater fish from the rivers in its food. Au pla is a menu item introduced as a local dish of Khon Kaen. It suits anyone who has tried som tam and larb, known across Isan, and wants to find out about another dish of Khon Kaen.
au-pla.tip: Eat slowly, checking for fish bones.
steps: Find au pla on the menu and ask which fish is used. It also helps to ask whether the heat can be adjusted.
Order rice to eat with it and take the fish and broth a little at a time.
Eat slowly, checking for fish bones. The kind of fish and the detailed seasoning depend on the menu item you order.
faq: How is it different from som tam or larb?
Au pla is a curry made with freshwater fish. Unlike som tam, in which papaya is pounded, or larb, in which minced meat is seasoned, you can eat the fish and broth over rice.
Is it a dish linked to Khon Kaen?
Yes. It is a menu item that the Tourism Authority of Thailand introduced as a local dish of Khon Kaen. If you want to try a freshwater fish dish on an Isan trip, you can take a look.

hat-yai-chicken.name: Hat Yai Fried Chicken
hat-yai-chicken.scope: The signature dish of Hat Yai
hat-yai-chicken.intro: In Hat Yai, try crunchy fried chicken with fried shallots on the side. It is Hat Yai fried chicken, known by the name of the city. The richness and aroma of the shallots are added to the crunchy chicken, and it goes well with sticky rice. Put a little of the shallots served with it on top of the chicken and take a bite.
hat-yai-chicken.flavor: It is a dish in which you enjoy the crunch of the fried chicken and the rich taste of shallots together. It is also characterised by seasoning with aromatics such as garlic, coriander root and white pepper. You can also try the chicken and shallots together before adding any sauce.
hat-yai-chicken.ingredients: Fried chicken with fried shallots on the side. It is known to be seasoned with garlic, coriander root, white pepper and so on, and eaten with sticky rice.
hat-yai-chicken.story: Hat Yai is a city in the Songkhla area, where the food culture of Chinese-descent and Muslim communities sits together. Hat Yai fried chicken is known as a signature dish of this area. It is sold in other cities too, but if you have come to Hat Yai, have it as a meal with sticky rice.
hat-yai-chicken.tip: Eat the fried shallots together with the chicken to enjoy the richness more.
steps: Choose the pieces and the quantity you want. If you are in a group, you can order the pieces you like and share them.
See whether sticky rice and sauce come with it, and order more of what you need.
First try the chicken and the fried shallots together. Next, add a little sauce and enjoy a different taste.
faq: Can I eat it only in Hat Yai?
No. Hat Yai-style fried chicken is sold in other areas too. If you have come to Hat Yai, you could try the dish known by the name of the city with sticky rice.
Is every chicken dish halal?
No. The kind of meat alone cannot decide whether a dish is halal. If you need a halal meal, look at the restaurant's certification together with the actual ingredients and cooking conditions.
hat-yai-chicken.photoAlt: Hat Yai-style fried chicken served with plenty of fried shallots
hat-yai-chicken.photoCaption: Hat Yai-style fried chicken · example dish

bak-kut-teh.name: Bak Kut Teh
bak-kut-teh.scope: A Chinese-descent dish enjoyed in the Songkhla area
bak-kut-teh.intro: If you want a meal of warm soup on a Hat Yai trip, choose bak kut teh. Pork ribs are simmered with herbs and aromatics. In the Songkhla area it is introduced as a soup dish with a Chinese-style herb aroma. If you eat pork, enjoy it slowly with rice.
bak-kut-teh.flavor: The aroma of herbs and aromatics is added to a broth in which pork ribs have been simmered. The colour and richness of the broth differ with the recipe. Alternate between the ribs and the broth to notice the aroma.
bak-kut-teh.ingredients: Pork ribs are simmered with herbs and aromatics. The other ingredients and accompaniments differ from menu item to menu item.
bak-kut-teh.story: Bak kut teh is one of the Chinese-descent dishes met in the Songkhla area. It does not mean that it was first made in Hat Yai. On a day when you want a meal different from crunchy fried chicken, have a meal of pork rib broth and rice.
bak-kut-teh.tip: The broth uses pork too. If you avoid pork, choose another dish.
steps: First think about whether it is a menu item for you and your companions, if they eat pork. The standard bak kut teh uses pork ribs.
Look at whether rice and accompaniments come with it, and order.
Eat the ribs and take the broth a little at a time. Enjoy it with rice, noticing the aroma of herbs and aromatics.
faq: Is bak kut teh a dish that began in Hat Yai?
It is not introduced as a dish of origin in Hat Yai. It is a Chinese-descent dish met in the Songkhla area, and a menu item through which you can learn about the area's varied food culture.
Can people who do not eat pork eat it?
The standard bak kut teh contains pork ribs. If you avoid pork, it is better to choose another dish. Please note that even if you eat only the broth, it is a dish made with pork.

roti.name: Roti
roti.intro: If you want something sweet from a street stall, try roti. Thinly stretched dough is cooked and served with a sweet sauce such as condensed milk or chocolate. Some menu items add banana, so it is a good choice when you want fruit and a snack together. If the roti is cut up for you, share it piece by piece while it is warm.
roti.flavor: You enjoy the taste of the thin cooked dough with the sweet sauce. Depending on what goes in and how it is cooked, the crunch at the edges and the softness inside change. In menu items with banana, you also feel the sweetness of the fruit.
roti.ingredients: Dough is cooked and served with sauce such as condensed milk or chocolate. Whether banana or egg goes in depends on the menu item.
roti.story: Roti in Thailand can also be met as a sweet street snack. Ayutthaya's roti sai mai is thin roti wrapped around sugar threads, and it is eaten differently from the cooked roti introduced here. Try both and you can enjoy different snacks under the one name of roti.
roti.tip: Banana and sauce depend on the menu item you order. Choose the topping you want first.
steps: Choose whether you want plain roti or roti with banana and so on, and tell them the sauce you want.
If you want less condensed milk or sauce, ask before it is cooked. Once the sauce has been drizzled on, it is hard to reduce the amount.
Share the cut roti piece by piece while it is warm.
faq: Is it the same snack as roti sai mai?
No. Roti sai mai is an Ayutthaya snack in which thin roti is wrapped around sugar threads. Here we introduce street roti, in which cooked dough is served with a sweet sauce.
Can I order it if I cannot eat egg or milk?
You need to ask about the ingredients in the dough, the toppings and the sauce together. Even a menu item without egg can have an ingredient you avoid in the dough or the condensed milk.
roti.photoCaption: Thai roti photographed at Bang Luang Mosque. Toppings and shape differ from shop to shop.

watermelon-shake.name: Watermelon Shake
watermelon-shake.intro: If you want a cold drink as you walk on a hot day in Thailand, try the watermelon shake, nam taeng mo pan. Watermelon is blended with water and ice. Unlike watermelon juice that you drink like plain juice, the ice is blended in together so you enjoy it cold. If you want less sweetness, say so when you order, asking for less syrup or sugar.
watermelon-shake.flavor: The cold, fine texture of blended ice is added to the taste of watermelon. The taste of one cup can change with the ratio of watermelon to ice and the sweetener added.
watermelon-shake.ingredients: Watermelon, water and ice are blended together. Additional ingredients such as sugar or syrup differ from seller to seller.
watermelon-shake.story: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces the watermelon shake as a typical fruit drink made by blending watermelon with water and ice. The familiar watermelon can be enjoyed as a street drink on a Thai trip. Watermelon is a fruit available all year round, but whether a shop actually sells the drink differs from shop to shop.
watermelon-shake.tip: If you want less sugar or syrup added, say so before it is made.
steps: Choose the watermelon shake and look at the cup size and the price.
Before the drink is made, ask whether the sweetness can be reduced. Even without syrup, the watermelon has its own sweetness.
When the drink blended with ice arrives, enjoy it while it is cold.
faq: Is it watermelon juice?
It is a shake made by blending watermelon with water and ice. Because the ice is blended in, the texture differs from a drink of pressed watermelon juice alone.
If I leave out the sugar, will it have no sweetness?
The watermelon's own sweetness remains. The sugar or syrup that adds sweetness differs from shop to shop, so ask before the drink is made for less or none.

mango.name: Mango
mango.availability: Listed as available all year round
mango.intro: If you want something sweet in Thailand, try a ripe mango. Varieties such as Nam Dok Mai are known for soft, fragrant yellow flesh. If you have had mango sticky rice, eat the fruit on its own and notice the taste of the mango itself. There are also kinds of unripe mango that are eaten crunchy and sour.
mango.taste: Ripe mango has a soft, sweet taste. Some green mango varieties are eaten for a texture different from ripe mango, so you need not assume that every green one is unripe just by its colour.
mango.why: Thailand has several mango varieties, such as Nam Dok Mai and Maha Chanok, and a food culture that enjoys ripe and green fruit in different ways. It is also familiar as the topping of a sticky rice dessert, so it is a fruit worth tasting on a Thai trip.
mango.buying: If you want sweet, soft mango, say that you are looking for ripe mango. Crunchy mango can also be sold separately. The price unit differs between buying whole fruit by the kg and buying a pack of sliced fruit.
steps: Wash whole fruit and cut off the flesh on both sides of the stone.
Cut the flesh into bite-sized pieces and eat it as it is, or enjoy it with mango sticky rice.
If you want to buy some to eat now and some to take away, choose the ripeness together with the seller.
mango.regional: Nam Dok Mai Si Thong of Phitsanulok: season listed as Mar–Jun
mango.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a mango. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

durian.name: Durian
durian.availability: Listed as available all year round
durian.intro: If its strong smell has made you hesitate, you can still try just a little durian. Inside the thorny rind is rich, yellow flesh. You taste the smooth, sweet flesh and its aroma together in one bite. If it is your first time, start at a place that sells a small amount of flesh rather than buying a whole fruit.
durian.taste: Its character is a sweet, rich taste and creamy flesh. The firmness and smell of the flesh differ with variety, such as Monthong and Chanee, and with ripeness.
durian.why: Thai durian varieties such as Monthong, Chanee and Kan Yao are well known. Because of its strong smell and sweet, rich flesh, it is also a fruit on which tastes divide sharply. You can eat it as it is, or enjoy it in ice cream and desserts.
durian.buying: First ask whether the price tag is per kg of whole fruit including the rind or per kg of prepared flesh. If you want to take it to a hotel or on transport, it is better to check the rules on bringing it in first.
steps: If it is your first time, buy a small amount of flesh and taste it.
If you choose a whole fruit, it is easier to get the variety, the ripeness and the price including the rind, and then ask for it to be prepared.
Leave out the large stone and eat the flesh. Before taking durian to your lodging, check whether it can be brought in.
durian.regional: Durian of the Sisaket volcanic area: season listed as May–Jun
durian.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a durian. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

mangosteen.name: Mangosteen
mangosteen.intro: Try mangosteen, whose purple rind opens to white flesh in segments. It tastes sweet and tangy together and is very juicy. Although mango is in its name, it is a different fruit from mango. It is also good to share a few with your companion after a meal.
mangosteen.taste: The white flesh is soft and sweet-sour. The larger segments can have a seed, so eat slowly.
mangosteen.why: Its appeal lies in the purple rind and white flesh and in a taste that is sweet yet fresh. In Thailand it comes into season at different times in different areas, so it is good to look for it to match the season you travel.
mangosteen.buying: Check whether the rind is damaged and choose fruit to eat right away. Because it is a whole fruit with a thick rind, the kg price is not the weight of the flesh you eat.
steps: Press the rind to open it, or cut the rind shallowly and open the inside.
Take out the white flesh and check for a seed inside the larger segments.
Be careful that the red juice from the rind does not stain your clothes as you eat.
mangosteen.regional: Khao Khiriwong mangosteen of the south: season listed as Jul–Dec
mangosteen.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a mangosteen. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

rambutan.name: Rambutan
rambutan.availability: The season differs by growing area
rambutan.intro: Meet rambutan, a red fruit whose rind has hair-like spines. Peel it and white flesh comes out, with sweet juice to enjoy. The look may be unfamiliar, but peeling it and taking out the stone is simple. You can also buy just a few at a market and taste them.
rambutan.taste: The white flesh is sweet and juicy. Some varieties, such as the Thai Rong Rian, differ in texture and in how easily the flesh comes away from the stone.
rambutan.why: The hairy-looking rind stands out, and white flesh is inside. The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces the Rong Rian rambutan of Na San, Surat Thani, as a regional GI fruit.
rambutan.buying: Ask whether it is sold by the kg or in a fixed bag. Choose only the amount you will eat right away, peel it and take out the stone.
steps: Make a shallow slit in the rind, then open it out and peel it.
Eat the white flesh, but remove the stone in the middle.
If it is sold in a bag, look at the weight and the price together before you buy.
rambutan.regional: Rong Rian rambutan of Na San: season listed as Jul–Aug

longan.name: Longan
longan.availability: Listed as available all year round
longan.intro: If you are curious about the fruit of Chiang Mai and the north, try longan. It is a small fruit with translucent flesh and a black stone inside a thin brown rind. Peel and eat them one at a time to enjoy the sweet taste. Dried longan and fresh fruit differ in texture, so you can taste the fresh fruit first.
longan.taste: The flesh is sweet, and the aroma differs with variety. There is a black stone inside the white flesh, so you take out the stone as you eat.
longan.why: It is a fruit that is easy to learn about in connection with northern Thailand. The Biao Kiao longan of Lamphun is introduced as a regional GI fruit, and the fruit is enjoyed dried as well as fresh.
longan.buying: Look at whether it is sold as a bunch including the stalks or as loose fruit. If you choose by the variety and weight on the price tag, it is easy to compare.
steps: Make a slit in the rind and peel it by hand.
Take out the black stone when you eat the flesh.
If you also want to buy a dried product, look at its price and pack weight separately from fresh fruit.
longan.regional: Biao Kiao longan of Lamphun: season listed as Jul–Sep
longan.photoCaption: Reference photo showing longan. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

lychee.name: Lychee
lychee.availability: The season differs by growing area and variety
lychee.intro: If you want a fragrant, juicy fruit, try lychee. Peel the red rind and white flesh comes out, and one bite gives sweet taste and aroma together. If you have had it in a drink or a dessert, you could also taste the fresh fruit in season.
lychee.taste: The white flesh is sweet, and depending on the variety you can also feel some sourness. You peel the rind and take out the stone in the middle.
lychee.why: Thai lychee varieties such as Hong Huay and Chakkaphat are well known. Kom lychee of Samut Songkhram is also introduced as a regional GI fruit, which makes it good for comparing fruit by growing area.
lychee.buying: Separate the units when whole fruit is sold by the kg and when it is sold in fixed packs. The season for lychee drinks on a menu and the sale of fresh fruit may not be the same.
steps: Peel the rind and take out the flesh.
Remove the stone in the middle and eat the flesh.
If you want to buy a pack to take home and some to eat right away separately, tell them the amount you need.
lychee.regional: Kom lychee of Samut Songkhram: season listed as Apr–May
lychee.photoCaption: Reference photo showing lychee. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

longkong.name: Longkong
longkong.availability: The season differs by growing area
longkong.intro: Meet longkong, small brownish fruit that hang in bunches. Peel the thin rind and translucent flesh comes out in segments. Even though the name is similar to longan, the shape and the way it eats are different. If you saw the two fruits side by side at a market, you could buy a little of each and compare.
longkong.taste: You can feel sweetness and some sourness in the translucent flesh. For a segment that has a seed, take the seed out instead of chewing it.
longkong.why: There is fun in peeling small fruit from the bunch one at a time. The Tan Yong Mat longkong of Narathiwat in the south is known as a regional GI fruit, so it is good to learn about it with its growing area.
longkong.buying: Longan and longkong are different fruits. If you order by looking at both the name and the look of the bunch, it is easy to get the fruit you want.
steps: Pull off one fruit from the bunch to eat.
Peel the rind and take out the flesh to eat.
The seed can taste bitter, so eat slowly and take out any seed you can see.
longkong.regional: Tan Yong Mat longkong: season listed as Aug–Sep

pomelo.name: Pomelo
pomelo.availability: Listed as available all year round
pomelo.intro: Try pomelo, which looks like a giant grapefruit. Peel off the thick rind and strip the inner skin, and the grains of flesh show. Sweetness and sourness feel different depending on the variety. If it is hard to use a knife at your lodging, you could choose pomelo that is sold prepared in a container.
pomelo.taste: It is a citrus fruit in which you can feel the grains of flesh. Colour, sweetness and sourness differ by variety, such as yellowish or pinkish flesh.
pomelo.why: Thailand has several pomelo varieties, such as Khao Nam Phueng and Thong Dee. Large whole fruit is also sold prepared with only the flesh in a container, so it is an easy fruit to taste while travelling.
pomelo.buying: Tell apart the price per fruit, the price per kg and the price of a prepared pack. A whole fruit with its rind and a pack of flesh only are hard to compare directly at the same weight.
steps: For a whole fruit, start by peeling off the thick outer rind.
Divide it into segments and strip the inner skin to take out the flesh.
Remove the seeds and eat the flesh. If you buy a prepared pack, it is easy to share right away.
pomelo.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a pomelo. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.availability: Listed as available all year round
pineapple.intro: On a hot day when you want a sweet and sour fruit, try pineapple. You can cut the yellow flesh and eat it piece by piece, or enjoy it as juice. Thailand has pineapples whose crunch and sweetness differ by variety and growing area. Instead of buying a whole fruit, you can also eat it simply from a bag of prepared pieces.
pineapple.taste: You feel sweetness and sourness together, and the firmness of the flesh differs with variety. If a seasoning is served on the side, taste the fruit first and then add it.
pineapple.why: It is grown in many parts of Thailand, and some regional fruit is introduced as GI, such as the Si Thong pineapple of Trat. It is familiar as whole fruit, prepared fruit and drinks alike.
pineapple.buying: First see whether it is the kg price of whole fruit, the price per fruit or the price of a bag of cut pieces. The preparation cost and the amount you eat differ.
steps: For whole fruit, prepare the rind and the hard parts before eating.
Cut it into bite-sized pieces to share, or choose a bag of prepared pieces.
If a seasoning is served with it, add a little at a time and eat it the way you like.
pineapple.regional: Si Thong pineapple of Trat: listed as available all year round
pineapple.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a pineapple. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

banana.name: Banana
banana.seasonLabel: A fruit to enjoy all year round
banana.availability: Differences by variety and growing area
banana.intro: In Thailand you can meet bananas of several shapes, from small ones upward. They are eaten as fresh fruit, and some menu items put them in roti or grill them. If you are looking for a simple snack on the street, also look at roti with banana.
banana.taste: Sweetness and the firmness of the flesh differ with variety and ripeness. It helps to tell apart bananas eaten when ripe and yellow and bananas used for cooking.
banana.why: It is a familiar fruit used in many Thai dishes and snacks. The Kluai Khai banana of Kamphaeng Phet is introduced as a regional GI fruit. If you have thought of only one kind of banana, look at the market for varieties of other shapes and sizes.
banana.buying: Bananas are sometimes sold by the bunch instead of by the kg. Look at how many are in a bunch, and if you will eat them right away, choose ripe bananas.
steps: Ask whether the price is for a bunch or for a set number of bananas.
Choose ripe bananas to eat right away, peel them and eat.
Banana roti and grilled banana are different menu items from whole fruit, so look at their prices separately.
banana.regional: Kluai Khai banana of Kamphaeng Phet: listed as available all year round
banana.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a banana. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

coconut.name: Young Coconut
coconut.availability: Listed as available all year round
coconut.intro: If you want cold coconut water on a hot day, choose a young coconut. Once the top is opened you drink the water inside, and you can spoon out the soft flesh too. The fragrant Nam Hom coconut is a known variety in Thailand. When you are thirsty, you can also share one with your companion.
coconut.taste: With a young coconut you enjoy the water and the soft white flesh together. Nam Hom is introduced as a variety whose character is its aroma.
coconut.why: The fragrant young coconut of Thailand is a fruit whose water you drink and whose flesh you eat. The fragrant coconut of Ban Phaeo in Samut Sakhon is also introduced as a regional GI fruit.
coconut.buying: Coconuts are sometimes sold one by one. Bottled coconut water and a coconut that is opened for you are not the same product, so look at the two menu items separately.
steps: Choose a coconut to drink right away and ask for the top to be opened.
After you drink the coconut water, if there is a spoon, scoop out the soft flesh too.
Order by telling apart the price of one coconut and the price of a bottled drink.
coconut.regional: Nam Hom coconut of Ban Phaeo: listed as available all year round
coconut.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a young coconut. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.availability: Listed as available all year round
watermelon.intro: In Thailand, enjoy watermelon as a drink too. Besides chilled slices, there is the watermelon shake, nam taeng mo pan, which is blended with ice. It is worth choosing on a day when you want a cold drink as you walk. If you want only the fruit, buy cut watermelon and share it with your companion.
watermelon.taste: It is a crunchy, juicy fruit. Fresh fruit and the shake blended with ice give you different textures.
watermelon.why: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces the watermelon shake as a typical fruit drink. Even a familiar fruit can be met on a trip in a different form, such as the watermelon shake.
watermelon.buying: Tell apart the kg price of a whole watermelon, a bag of cut watermelon and a cup of watermelon shake. Even when the same watermelon is used, the preparation and the amount in the drink differ.
steps: Cut a whole watermelon into bite-sized pieces and pick out the seeds as you eat.
When you eat right away on your trip, you can also choose cut watermelon in a container.
If you order the watermelon shake, say before the drink is made whether the sweetness can be reduced.
watermelon.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a watermelon. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

papaya.name: Papaya
papaya.availability: Listed as available all year round
papaya.intro: If you have tried som tam in Thailand, taste ripe papaya too. Unlike the green papaya used in som tam, ripe flesh is eaten soft and sweet. Cut it in half, scoop out the black seeds and eat the flesh. When you choose cut fruit, you could also look for ripe papaya.
papaya.taste: Ripe papaya is a fruit in which you enjoy soft flesh. Unripe papaya is also used as a cooking ingredient, so its texture differs from papaya eaten as fruit.
papaya.why: It is a familiar fruit through som tam, the green papaya salad. In Thailand you can learn both how to eat the ripe fruit and how to use the unripe fruit in dishes.
papaya.buying: Tell apart ripe papaya to eat right away as fruit and green papaya to use in a dish, and choose accordingly. The price unit can also differ between whole fruit and a prepared pack.
steps: Wash a ripe papaya and cut it in half.
Scoop out the black seeds in the middle, peel it and eat the flesh.
Green papaya and ripe papaya are eaten differently, so choose the one you will eat right away.
papaya.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a papaya. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

tamarind.name: Sweet Tamarind
tamarind.availability: The season differs by growing area and variety
tamarind.intro: Try sweet tamarind, which is inside a brown pod. Open the pod and strip the fibres from the flesh, and you can eat the soft pulp. If you knew tamarind only as an ingredient in the tangy sauce of Pad Thai, meet the sweet tamarind eaten as a fruit too.
tamarind.taste: Sweet tamarind is a fruit eaten soft and sweet. Take out the hard stone and the fibres in the middle and eat the flesh.
tamarind.why: Apart from the tamarind that gives dishes their sourness, there are varieties enjoyed as sweet fruit. The sweet tamarind of Phetchabun is introduced as a regional GI fruit.
tamarind.buying: Tell apart fresh fruit in the pod and packaged products with the stone removed or processed. Even for the same tamarind, the product and pack weight differ.
steps: Crack the pod and take out the flesh.
Take out the attached fibres and the hard stone as you eat the flesh.
A processed product has a different price unit from fresh fruit, so choose by looking at the weight of the pack.
tamarind.regional: Sweet tamarind of Phetchabun: season listed as Nov–Apr
tamarind.photoCaption: Reference photo showing sweet tamarind. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

mandarin.name: Thai Mandarin Orange
mandarin.availability: Listed as available all year round
mandarin.intro: If you see a citrus fruit with green rind in Thailand, you need not think it is unripe just from its colour. The rind and taste of mandarin oranges differ by variety. Easy to peel by hand and eat segment by segment, it is a fruit worth choosing to share simply on your trip.
mandarin.taste: You enjoy the sweetness and acidity of citrus together. The taste differs with variety and ripeness, and the flesh can have seeds.
mandarin.why: Thailand has several mandarin orange varieties. The golden orange of Nan is introduced among regional GI fruit for its green rind and sweet-sour taste.
mandarin.buying: Compare kg prices that carry a variety and a size grade only within the same grade. Beyond the rind colour, you can also choose fruit to eat right away together with the seller.
steps: Peel the rind and divide it into segments to eat.
For a variety with seeds, take out the seeds as you eat.
Look separately at the price of products sold as juice and the kg price of whole fruit.
mandarin.regional: Golden orange of Nan: season listed as Nov–Dec
mandarin.photoCaption: Reference photo showing a Thai mandarin orange. It is not limited to the Thai growing areas and varieties described in the text.

marian-plum.name: Mayongchid · Marian Plum
marian-plum.availability: Season given for the regional fruit
marian-plum.intro: If you see a small, yellowish fruit that looks like a little mango in Thailand, ask whether it is mayongchid. It is a fruit of the plum mango group, and the mayongchid of Nakhon Nayok is introduced as a regional GI fruit. If you want to try a fruit different from large mangoes, you could look for it in winter and early spring.
marian-plum.taste: The Nakhon Nayok mayongchid is introduced as having sweet and sour notes together with crunchy flesh. Take out the stone in the middle and eat.
marian-plum.why: The Tourism Authority of Thailand introduces the mayongchid of Nakhon Nayok as a regional GI fruit. You can learn about a small fruit that looks similar to mango together with its growing area.
marian-plum.buying: Even among similar plum mango types, the varieties and names differ. It helps to say that you are looking for mayongchid and get the actual variety and price.
steps: Wash the fruit you bought and cut it into bite-sized pieces.
Take out the stone in the middle and eat the flesh.
There may be other varieties with a similar name to mayongchid, so show the name of the fruit you want to buy.
